title: Stem Cell Therapy (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand in plain words what stem cells are, what approved treatments exist, how to spot unproven clinics, and the ethics involved. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what stem cells are and the main types.
Use a checklist to judge a clinic or advert.
Separate approved uses from experimental claims.
Weigh hope against evidence and cost.
Draft a short guide for patients and families.
task: Produce a one-page safe-choice guide on stem cell treatments with a clinic checklist and a glossary.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. No medical advice is given and no patient records are used.
standard: Facts are sourced and dated; approved and experimental uses are kept apart; no promise of cure appears; the guide tells readers to ask a qualified specialist; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Patients, carers, teachers, health writers and trainee lab staff.
modules: What stem cells are
Understand
Stem cells can copy themselves and can become other kinds of cell. That is why they matter in medicine.
Types: embryonic (from early embryos), adult or tissue (in bone marrow, skin, gut) and induced (adult cells reprogrammed in a lab).
Each type has different uses, limits and ethical questions.
Your body already uses stem cells every day, for example to renew blood and skin.
A stem cell in a lab is not a treatment until it has passed regulated testing.
Blood stem cells in bone marrow keep making new red cells, white cells and platelets throughout life. A donor transplant replaces a patient's marrow when it is damaged.
Draw a picture of one stem cell dividing into one copy and one specialised cell, and label three types.
Picture is accurate and labels are correct.
Established and approved uses
Understand
Some stem cell treatments are established. Many claims are not.
Blood stem cell transplants are used for certain blood cancers and inherited blood disorders.
Skin grafts and corneal surface treatments using stem cells exist for some conditions.
Approval means regulators reviewed trial evidence for a named condition.
Most other uses are experimental and belong in registered trials.
A hospital matches a patient with a donor, checks tissue types, gives the transplant under specialist care and follows up for years. This is regulated, documented and repeatable.
List three approved uses and name a public source for each.
Sources are regulators or recognised hospitals and are dated.
Trials and evidence
Analyse
Medicine moves from idea to approval in stages, and each stage reduces risk.
Stages: laboratory work, small safety trials, larger effectiveness trials, regulator review, approval, monitoring.
Patient stories are not proof; control groups and large numbers are.
Registered trials appear in public registries.
Ask: Is this approved, or is it in a registered trial?
A clinic advertises success stories only. The learner searches a trial registry and finds no registered trial for the claimed condition, so rates the claim unproven.
Check one claim in a public trial registry and write the result.
Result states registry searched, terms used and date.
Spotting unproven clinics
Evaluate
Some clinics sell hope at high prices without evidence. Families can lose money and delay real care.
Red flags: cures many unrelated diseases, pay in advance, no registered trial, no follow-up, pressure to decide fast.
Risks include infection, unwanted growths and lost time.
Ask for the approval or trial number and check it yourself.
Talk to your own specialist before travelling.
A family is offered an injection costing a year's income for a condition with no approved stem cell treatment. They ask for the trial number, receive none, and decline.
Score two real adverts with the red-flag list and justify each score.
Each score cites the advert wording.
Ethics and sources
Evaluate
People hold different views on where cells come from and how they should be used.
Donors must give informed and free consent, with the right to withdraw.
Embryo use is debated; religions and cultures differ.
Cord blood banking is a personal choice with limited current uses.
Fairness: who can afford treatment, and who does research benefit?
A parents' guide explains cord blood choices, costs and the limits of use without pressure and tells parents to ask their doctor.
Write a balanced paragraph on one ethical question presenting two views fairly.
Both views are stated in terms their holders would accept.
Talking with specialists
Apply
A prepared patient gets better answers.
Questions: what is this for, is it approved, what are the risks, what does it cost, what are the alternatives, what follow-up is needed.
Bring a family member and take notes.
Second opinions are normal.
Ask for written information.
A patient brings a one-page question list to the haematologist, gets written answers and decides after a second opinion.
Prepare a question list of at least eight questions for a specialist visit.
Questions are clear and cover approval, risk, cost and follow-up.
Cost, travel and safety
Evaluate
Medical travel adds risks beyond the procedure.
Check licence of clinic and doctor in the destination.
Count the full cost: fee, flights, stay, follow-up at home, complications.
Plan who provides follow-up care when you return.
Keep records of everything given.

A traveller totals fee 12,00,000 INR (figures are estimates; check current prices), flights and stay 1,50,000 INR, and complication cover 2,00,000 INR (total 15,50,000 INR), then decides against it after comparing with an approved local option.
Cost a hypothetical trip and list five safety questions.
Total includes all cost items with currency.
Write the safe-choice guide
Create
Turn the course into one useful page for patients and families.
One page, plain words, large print.
Include the clinic checklist and local regulator contacts.
Add a glossary of five terms.
Test with two readers and fix confusing parts.
Readers say they would first ask "is it in a registered trial?" and know where to look it up.
Finish the guide and test it.
Readers can repeat three red flags without notes.
quiz: Name two stem cell types.
Adult (tissue) and embryonic (or induced). (Covered in module 1: What stem cells are. To pass that module: Picture is accurate and labels are correct.)
Name one long-established use.
Blood stem cell transplant for some blood disorders. (Covered in module 2: Established and approved uses. To pass that module: Sources are regulators or recognised hospitals and are dated.)
Are patient stories proof?
No. (Covered in module 3: Trials and evidence. To pass that module: Result states registry searched, terms used and date.)
Name two red flags.
Cures many diseases; pay up front or fast pressure. (Covered in module 4: Spotting unproven clinics. To pass that module: Each score cites the advert wording.)
What question tests a clinic?
Is it approved or in a registered trial? (Covered in module 3: Trials and evidence. To pass that module: Result states registry searched, terms used and date.)
Name one risk.
Infection, tumours, wasted money or delayed care. (Covered in module 4: Spotting unproven clinics. To pass that module: Each score cites the advert wording.)
Why consent?
Donors must freely agree with full information. (Covered in module 5: Ethics and sources. To pass that module: Both views are stated in terms their holders would accept.)
Is a second opinion normal?
Yes. (Covered in module 6: Talking with specialists. To pass that module: Questions are clear and cover approval, risk, cost and follow-up.)
What cost parts does travel add?
Flights, stay and follow-up. (Covered in module 7: Cost, travel and safety. To pass that module: Total includes all cost items with currency.)
Who gives medical advice?
Qualified specialists, not this course. (Covered in module 6: Talking with specialists. To pass that module: Questions are clear and cover approval, risk, cost and follow-up.)
rubric: Each treatment is marked approved, trial-only or unproven, with source
Each stage is checked against a public register on a stated date
Checklist covers licence, approval, advertised cures and fees
Checklist tried on two real clinic websites, with findings recorded
